George
Be n s o n
From the very beginning,
the sound of the guitar
was always in my mind.
From the moment I heard
it, I knew that my life was
going to have something
to do with the guitar. I did
not know I was going to be
a player yet, but I loved the
sound.
                                    68
                           46




 As I grew older, I began to dabble with the guitar, to pick it up and try to pick things out. I would get so far, and
 then I would get stuck. I have found later that this is normal. Everybody goes through that on every instrument.
 To move forward, you have to take in more information, and look at things from different angles or from a dif-
 ferent point of view. So I started asking questions from the people whom I knew that had a certain mastery of the
 instrument.

 In my home town of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, a lot of traveling groups would come through town and I always went up
 to the guitar player to ask if he could show me something. I was never too ashamed to ask. The George Benson you
 know today is a collection of all those people who took the time to show me what they knew, and the things I could
 hang on to did me a lot of good.

 From guitar books, which I was not a reader, I was more of a picture guy. But the demonstrations in the new books
 really helped a lot to show the correct fingerings for this, that, and the other. They showed how to make chords.
 The chords led me to the harmony, that helped me to become a better single line player.

       Peter Farrell
                                  68
                           46




          Peter Farrell was born in Sao Paulo, Brazil in 1981. Son of the singer Claudia Fier and the
          saxophone player Lino Simão. He began studying music at school very young with an early
          interest in flute & violin.

          Still very young, his mother introduced him to the jazz and classical worlds, giving him the
          opportunity to hear the music of George Benson, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Debussy, Ravel,
          Bach, Dori Caymmi, Toninho Horta, Bill Evans, Herbie Hancock and many others.

          However, just like every teenager, Peter loved rock’n’roll and at the age of 11 he asked his
          mother to take him to a guitar teacher. So he began studying guitar with José Walter, which
          gave him the first basic steps to rock and blues.

                                2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
the George Benson Method                                                                                    4668




            One year later, the young boy was taken by his aunt Léa Freire and his uncle Sizão Mach-
            ado to a music conservatory called Groove, where he studied classical guitar, music
            theory, and jazz guitar with Leyve Miranda and Luis Cavalcante. In this period Peter
            started going deep into the music of George Benson and Wes Montgomery.

            Also in this period, Peter studied Brazilian music with the extraordinary guitar player Lula
            Galvão, and also piano with the great pianist and arranger Edmundo Cassis, who gave him
            a new vision about harmony.

            After many years of studying day and night, Peter started giving his first lessons and re-
            alized he had a great talent to teach and encourage others. Since then teaching has also
            become his passion.

            It did not take long until musicians all over the world started keeping their eyes on him
            because of his ability, technique and musicality. He was very advanced for an 18 year old
            boy. As a matter of fact, Peter was known in the musical scene as a prodigy since he was 14.

            Sometime later Peter was introduced to his idol and mentor George Benson. The connec-
            tion between them was instantaneous. The great Benson was amazed at Peter’s talent and
            how he had decoded many of his secrets. After a few months of friendship, Peter became
                                    68


            Mr. Benson’s private student and it has continued for the past 15 years.

            During the last six years Peter Farrell and George Benson have been dedicated to this col-
                           46




            lection of method books that they have created together: The George Benson Method.

            Peter Farrell has recorded and played with many great artists all over the world such as Jane
            Monheit, Brian McKnight, Eumir Deodato, Cesar Camargo Mariano, Romero Lubambo,
            Adam Rogers, and Didier Lockwood just to name a few.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.


George and I have been working for many years on this giant collection of books to give you the
best we can and help those that love the guitar the way we do. We hope this method can open a
                               68


new world that was unknown until now. You have a treasure in your hands. It contains all the
knowledge that George Benson has been teaching me privately over the last 15 years.
                      46




Thanks a lot,


Peter Farrell

                                               Important device:
The patterns and scale visualizations in this book may have different time signatures in order to
help with the organization and visualization. Notice that depending on where and how we play
them on the fretboard, we will have more or less possibilities. Don’t let the time signatures
confuse you. Learn the ideas that you like the most and apply them where you feel they sound
the best. Give more attention to the single lines shown.


                                          2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
Organizing the Blues Studies                                                                           4668




The Blues is one of the most important musical pillars for those who want to learn how to
improvise. First because we can learn so much about how to "tell a story" using melodies and
rhythmic ideas. Second because over this wonderful form we can apply and find endlees
harmonic possibilities and substitutions, which will change the way we see improvisation.

In this Book we will learn how to create and apply all the melodic material we have learned
previously over the blues form. But to better organize the studies, let's split the blues into three
different worlds:



1) FAST TEMPOS;

2) MEDIUM TEMPOS;

3) SLOW TEMPOS.



1) FAST TEMPOS:

With Fast Tempos we will improve our reasoning speed and of course the right & left-hand
technique thus giving us more fluency with the connections between scales and all the ideas we
                               68


have been learning.
                      46




2) MEDIUM TEMPOS:

With the Medium Tempos we will be using all the time a very special and unique technique that
we have learned previously called inverted hammer or also called reverse hammer. Also, in this
type of tempo, we will learn how to breathe between the melodies thus giving the solo a
different vibe and context.


3) SLOW TEMPOS:

This is the most difficult tempo to master and improvise because we will be using what we call
"Rhythmic Positioning", which combines all types of time feel and rhythmic cells we have been
working on. John Coltrane used to say that the secret of the improvisation can be found over
balllads, so let's keep this idea alive.

                                                                                                       1
                             2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
    The Pre-set choruses
                                                                                                        4668




    To better internalize the melodic, harmonic and rhythmic possibilities for each blues tempo, we
    will give you some pre-set choruses which combine all the material we have been studying in
    the previous GB Method Books such as Blues ideas, Double Stops, Pure Major 7th & Minor 7th
    ideas, superimposition possibilities, Dorian, Harmonic Minor and Melodic Minor ideas, Bebop
    Scales & Symmetric Scales ideas.

    Although there is no need to memorize all the pre-set choruses, you should analyze all of them,
    mainly to learn the harmonic and melodic possibilities and ideas we can have for each part of
    the blues form.


    Note: Choose the choruses you like the most and try to make some combinations between them.
          There are arrows with explanations for every line presented in these pre-set choruses thus
          making everything easy and fun.




    Telling a Story/ Creativity
                                  68



    As we know, the blues is divided into three "stories". The magic of creativity will happen when
                         46




    after memorizing some choruses we start combining them. With three choruses, for example,
    we can have a lot of fun. See below:

    • 1, 1, 1 (means that we are playing the complete chorus 1)
    • 2, 2, 2 (means that we are playing the complete chorus 2)
    • 3, 3, 3 (means that we are playing the complete chorus 3)
    • 1, 2, 3 (means that we are combining the first part of chorus 1
      with the second part of chorus 2 and the resolution of chorus 3)


    Obviously, you will have to adapt and work in every combination between blues choruses you
    make, because some of them might not fit one another. For example, for some combinations we
    will have to take out determined line to better connect the ideas. Takes time, but you will learn
    a lot by doing this process.

Tools Check List:
                                                                                                                 4668




Below we have a list of things that we must know before we jump to the studies of this book. It
isnot necessary to know everything from each subject (first because it would not be possible),
but it is extremely important to understand the concepts and how to use them properly. In the
case of harmony, you must at least know the basic chords and where they come from (chord
families). In the case of the melodic lines, you must at least memorize a few line examples
using each one of the presented scales.

Notice that some scales below make part of the same mode. However, they must be visualized
differently according to each situation that might appear. For example, when we talk about "G"
Major Phrygian, of course we are talking about "C" Harmonic Minor Scale. When we are
talking about "F" Lydian Dominant Scale, we are talking about "C" Melodic Minor Scale. But
as we mentioned before, depending on the situation you must visualize one of them or maybe
both at the same time.

• Major                         • Pentatonnic/ Blues Scale                          • Chord Families (all)
• Minor                         • The Secret of the 2 Chords                        • Harmonic Regions
• Major 7th                     • Natural Major Scale (Ionian)                      • II, V, I (major & minor)
• Dominant 7th                  • Natural Minor Scale (Aeolian)                     • Turnarounds
                              68


• Minor 7th                     • Dorian Scale                                      • Diminished Chords
• Minor 6th                     • Mixolydian Scale                                  • Tritone Substitutions
                     46

• Half diminished               • Major Phrygian

                                • Dominant Diminished
                                • Outside major 7th Chords


Do not try to skip any step, otherwise you will get lost and will not learn properly. In case you
don't know some of the subjects above, we recommend you to get the previous GB Method
Books to better guide you. If you are OK with the subjects, welcome to the party!

                            2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
    Rhythmic Positioning                                                                                          4668




    Although some people think that the secret of jazz is the pulse 2 and 4, actually it is the opposite.
    The real Jazz feeling has its pillar in 1 and 3. But what about the 2 and the 4? Guess what, the
    stronger we feel the 1 and 3, the easier we can feel the pulse in 2 and 4.

    If we come back in time, specifically in the Dixieland era (Dixieland is a subgenre of Jazz
    created in 1910, in New Orleans), we can really understand where the idea of 1 and 3 came
    from. Although some people can just consider it as a dead style, this is much more than that
    because it gave Jazz a pillar to structure all the modern things we do nowadays.

    Based on that, let's split what we call rhythmic positioning into 5 types:

    1) Slow Blues Vibe
    2) Funk Vibe
    3) African Vibe
    4) Boogaloo Vibe
    5) Free Slow Blues Vibe


    "The Dance of the Elephant"

    Before we start learning the rhythmic groove ideas let's understand an extremely important thing:
    "the dance of the elephant" which is to move your body from one side to the other just like an
    elephant walks. See the example below:
                                    68


                     (off beat)                  (off beat)                    (off beat)            (off beat)
                         ¿                           ¿                             ¿                     ¿
                      rebound                     rebound                       rebound               rebound
     44
            œ                        œ                              œ                         œ
                             46




           1                        2                              3                         4
           move                    move                           move                       move
          to the                  to the                         to the                     to the
           left                   right                           left                      right

    Note: We feel the rebound always except in the slow blues vibe where the beats are divided in 3.


    Attention: The drum's rhythmic groove ideas on the next page are just to exemplify the correct
    vibe of each rhythmic positioning. In the songs suggested the bass and drums might be a little
    different but still make part of the suggested grooves.

    Melodic Studies
          68

        2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
                                                                                                      4668




Attention:

Before we jump to the pre-set blues choruses, let's understand and practice some melodic
possibilities for each part of the blues form. It is extremely important to understand that we
should not study the whole form at once. If we really want to master it, we must study each part
and each possibility separately to make them part of ourselves.


Of course, after studying some melodic possibilities, it will be important to play the whole blues
form, but we will be doing that later when we start studying the pre-set choruses in the next
pages.


For now, we will give you many possibilities of chord substitutions thus giving you a kind of
"menu" of new melodic ideas to choose and memorize. However, after learning some of them,
we should practice improvising not only using the line ideas we have memorized, but the
harmonic concept on it. The lines are extremely important, no doubt, but the idea is not to
become a "parrot" but a wise improviser that creates new combinations derived from a single
line.


As we will be improvising using new concepts and fresh ideas, we should do it over a slow
medium tempo backing track (110 bpm works fine). After getting used to some new possibilities,
                               68


we should do the same process using faster tempos and slower tempos. Fast tempos demand a lot
of patience and resilience, so naturally it will be much more difficult to improvise breaking and
combining your lines. That is why we also must study, memorize and combine some pre-set
                      46




choruses, not only melodically speaking but in terms of fingering, picking and line combinations.


In other words, if we want to reach our goal we must study and master many things, not only
one. Also, it is important to mention that we do not have to play fast tempos if we do not like it.
But we must understand that playing fast is a consequence, not a goal.


On the next pages, we will start the journey of fresh and new ideas taken from masters of
improvisation such as Charlie Parker, Wes Montgomery, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk, Bud
Powell, Grant Green, Cannonball Adderley and so many others. We hope that you enjoy it a lot
just like we had a lot of fun creating this book for you guys. Enjoy the Trip!!!

3) Superimposed Major 7th Chord Tricks                                                                                                                                     4668




In the following examples we will combine dominant 7th ideas (Blues Scale, Mixolydian and
Lydian Dominant Scales) with superimposition of major 7th arpeggios over dominant 7th chords.
Basic Harmony: ||                       F7                  |                  Bb7            |                F7                |               %                    ||

       Option 1: ||                 Ebmaj7                  |              Bb7                |                F7                |               %                    ||
                              Ebmaj7 contains all the
                              extended notes from F7
                               (7th, 9th, 11th, 13th).
                            Although it works perfectly,
                            we should sometimes apply
                             the note "A" which is the
                                major third of "F".

About Gbmaj7 replacing Bb7:
In this case we are replacing Bb7 (Subdominant Region chord) by Gbmaj7, which is a chord derived from the Subdominant Minor (Bm)
of the tonality (F).

About Emaj7 replacing Bb7:
Just like we learned before, leading dominant 7th chord substitution rules can work to lead us to major or minor chords. In other words,
the harmonic region rules we have learned as connected to minor tonalities can also work for major tonalities when we talk about
dominant 7th chord substitutions. Based on that, let's remember that for minor tonalities the dominant chord can be replaced by any
Minor Subdominant Region chord or any Minor Subdominant Region chord derived from the relative of the minor tonality. In this case,
the tonality is Fm and its relative is Ab major. Now let's get the Minor Subdominant Region chords from Ab major: Dbm (7, maj7, 6),
Gb7, Emaj7... ops, here is the chord we are talking about.

5) Superimposed IIm7/V7/I Cadences Over                                                            4668




   Dominant 7th Chords
Although we can apply any leading dominant 7th scale over the V degree of a IIm7, V7, I
cadence, when we superimpose them things are quite different because the V7 degree cannot
have tensions anymore thus becoming part of the IIm7 degree dorian.

In other words, in general the superimposed IIm7, V7, I cadences lose the V degree and stay
only with the IIm7 and the Imaj7. However, remember that we can always use the relative
chords from minor and major chords.


Example:

Let's look at cadence in the key of "C" (Dm7, G7, Cmaj7). Therefore we would have 4 different
"colors" to use as superimposition ideas:

• Dm7, Fmaj7 (relative of Dm7) Cmaj7 and Am7 (relative of Cmaj7).

Usually hybrid ideas tend to sound better. However, we can use Dorian ideas over the IIm7 of a
cadence and use Lydian ideas over its relative chord, which will be the IV degree (in this case,
Fmaj7).

Notice that we have an exception which is when the V degree of the superimposed cadence is
the Tritone Substitution from a real dominant chord in the harmony. Then we can choose
                              68


between 2 scales: Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished.
                     46




Let's get D7 leading to Gm7 as an example:

In this case we could have the superimposed cadence Ebm7, Ab7, Dbmaj7 used over D7. But
remember that we can always use the 3 chords from this cadence with their relative chords
individually. Apart from that, Ab7 is a Tritone Substitution from D7, which allows us to play
Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished ideas over it.


Therefore, in this example we can have 5 different “colors” to use superimposing D7:

1) Ebm7 (Dorian or hybrid)
2) Gbmaj7 - relative of Ebm7 - ( Lydian or hybrid)
3) Dbmaj7 (hybrid)
4) Bbm7 - relative of Dbmaj7 - (hybrid)
5) Ab7 (Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished)

                                                                                                   35
                            2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
     Basic Harmony: ||                                  F7                 |      Bb7                      |              F7               |          %            ||     4668




              Option 1: ||                              F7                 |     Bb7                       |                 F7            | F#m7           B7 ||
                                                                                                                                               (Amaj7)

     2nd possibility: ||                                F7                 |      Bb7                      |             F#m7              |          B7             ||
                                                                                                                         (Amaj7)                Lydian Dominant or
                                                                                                                                               Dominant Diminished
     About the cadence F#m7, B7 & Amaj7 replacing F7:
     F#m7, B7: In this case, F#m7 and B7 can be considered a single F#m7 Dorian chord. However, as mentioned before, in this case we
     can use some dominant 7th scales over B7 because it is the Tritone Substitution for F7 which is the real dominant 7th chord leading us
     to Bb7.
     Amaj7: Is the relative of F#m7 which is part from the cadence F#m7, B7 that replace F7 leading to Bb7. As a major chord not derived
     from the chord family of the tonality, Amaj7 ahould be treated as a Lydian chord. However we can use Amaj7 hybrid or Lydian ideas
     superimposing F7 chord leading to Bb7.

              Option 3: ||                 F7              |          Bb7                  |           F7         | C#m7               F#7 ||
                                                                                                                      (Emaj7)

       2nd possibility: ||                 F7              |           Bb7                 |       C#m7           |         F#7               ||
                                                                                                   (Emaj7)
     About the cadence C#m7(Emaj7), F#7 replacing F7:
     C#m7, F#7: In this case, C#m7 and F#7 can be considered a single C#m7 Dorian chord. However, we cannot forget that we do not have
     to play always C#m7 Dorian lines, we can also play C#m7 hybrid lines over F7. Notice that the hybrid lines from C#m7 contains the
     altered tensions of F7 (#9, b9, #11, b13). Also notice that C#m7 Dorian will give a special flavor to "F7" because of two specific notes:
     "E" and "A#" (minor 3rd and major 6th of C#m7 & major 7th and perfect 4th of "F"). Apart from that, C#m7 Dorian can work as a
     substitution possibility for C7 leading to Fm7, which works together with Bb7 Mixolydian.

     Emaj7 replacing F7: This chord appears in two superimposed cadences that can be applied over F7. It appears as a resolution of F#m7,
      B7, and as a relative chord from the II degree of the cadence C#m7, F#7, Bmaj7. In theory, Emaj7 should be treated as a Lydian chord
     because it is not derived from the chord family of the tonality (F). However this is an exception, and the best solution would be using
     Emaj7 hybrid lines, as these notes are the tension notes from F7 (#9, b9, #11, b13).
     Note: This is not a rule, we might have some exceptions.

     About Bmaj7 replacing F7:
     Bmaj7 is the resolution chord from the cadence C#m7, F#7 that can replace F7 leading to Bb7. Melodically speaking, Bmaj7 chord
     must be treated as a Lydian chord, however we can also use hybrid ideas over it. Notice that the Bmaj7 Lydian scale contains the
     altered tensions from F7 (#9, b9, #11, b13). Also it can give a special flavor to F7 because of the note Bb (A#), which is the major 7th
     from "B" and the perfect 4th from "F".

     About Bm7 replacing F7:
     In this case Bm7 should be considered Dorian because it is a minor chord not derived from the chord family of the tonality. Actually,
     Bm7 Dorian is a combination between "F" Dominant Diminished and "F" Altered Scale that can lead us to Bb7 (next chord of the
     blues form).

          Option 4: ||                          Bb7                         |               Bº               |              Fmaj7             |                   D7            ||
                                                                                                                       In this case we are
                                                                                                                     replacing the key (F7)
About Bº replacing Bb7:                                                                                                     by Fmaj7
In this case we are replacing the Subdominant Region chord Bb7 by a diminished chord working as C7 (Dominant Region chord)
leading to Fmaj7 (key). But let's understand this substitution step by step: B° is the same chord as F° which is actually the same chord
as E7 with a different bass note. Therefore, we would have E7 leading to Fmaj7. Notice that all the notes from E7 (except the flat 7th)
are half step from the notes of Fmaj7, which means that we would have many leading notes working together to reach the tonality (F).
But we still have to analyze the flat 7th of "E". First of all, it is important to understand that a leading note sometimes can be a whole
step, not exactly a half step as usual. Actually it is a process of understanding where a note wants to go. So, the "D" note (b7th of "E")
can work as a leading note to "E" (major 7th of "F").

         Option 5: ||                Bb7                 |       Amaj7                |          Dm7              |        D7           ||
                                                             Replacing Bb7 (IV)           IVm replacing the key
About Amaj7 replacing Bb7:
First of all, we have to understand that leading dominant 7th chord substitution rules can work to lead us to major or minor chords.
In other words, the harmonic region rules we have learned as connected to minor tonalities can also work for major tonalities when
we talk about dominant 7th chord substitutions. Based on that, let's remember that for minor tonalities, the dominant chord can be
replaced by any Minor Subdominant Region chord or any Minor Subdominant Region chord derived from the relative of the minor
tonality. In this case, the tonality is Fm and its relative is Ab major. Now let's get the Minor Subdominant Region chords from Ab
major: Dbm (7, maj7, 6), Gb7, Emaj7 and Amaj7... ops, here is the chord we are talking about. So, in theory we could use all those
chords as substitution chords to C7 leading to Fm or F major. As a major chord not derived from the tonality, Amaj7 can be
considered Lydian or •hybrid (• no mode involved).

         Option 6: ||                   Bb7                       |             Emaj7                 |        Fmaj7              |          D7                  ||
About Emaj7 replacing Bb7:
Just like we have learned before, leading dominant 7th chord substitution rules can work to lead us to major or minor chords. In other
words, the harmonic region rules we have learned as connected to minor tonalities can also work for major tonalities when we talk
about dominant 7th chord substitutions. Based on that, let's remember that for minor tonalities, the dominant chord can be replaced by
any Minor Subdominant Region chord or any Minor Subdominant Region chord derived from the relative of the minor tonality. In this
case, the tonality is Fm and its relative is Ab major. Now let's get the Minor Subdominant Region chords from Ab major: Dbm
(7,maj7,6), Gb7, Emaj7... ops, here is the chord we are talking about. As a major chord not derived from the tonality, Amaj7 can be
considered lydian or •hybrid (• no mode involved).

5) Superimposed IIm7/V7/I Cadences Over                                                            4668




   Dominant 7th Chords
Although we can apply any leading dominant 7th scale over the V degree of a IIm7, V7, I
cadence, when we superimpose them things are quite different because the V7 degree cannot
have tensions anymore thus becoming part of the IIm7 degree dorian.

In other words, in general the superimposed IIm7, V7, I cadences lose the V degree and stay
only with the IIm7 and the Imaj7. However, remember that we can always use the relative
chords from minor and major chords.


Example:

Let's look at cadence in the key of "C" (Dm7, G7, Cmaj7). Therefore we would have 4 different
"colors" to use as superimposition ideas:

• Dm7, Fmaj7 (relative of Dm7) Cmaj7 and Am7 (relative of Cmaj7).

Usually hybrid ideas tend to sound better. However, we can use Dorian ideas over the IIm7 of a
cadence and use Lydian ideas over its relative chord, which will be the IV degree (in this case,
Fmaj7).

Notice that we have an exception which is when the V degree of the superimposed cadence is
the Tritone Substitution from a real dominant chord in the harmony. Then we can choose
                             68


between 2 scales: Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished.
                    46




Let's get D7 leading to Gm7 as an example:

In this case we could have the superimposed cadence Ebm7, Ab7, Dbmaj7 used over D7. But
remember that we can always use the 3 chords from this cadence with their relative chords
individually. Apart from that, Ab7 is a Tritone Substitution from D7, which allows us to play
Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished ideas over it.


Therefore, in this example we can have 5 different “colors” to use superimposing D7:

1) Ebm7 (Dorian or hybrid)
2) Gbmaj7 - relative of Ebm7 - ( Lydian or hybrid)
3) Dbmaj7 (hybrid)
4) Bbm7 - relative of Dbmaj7 - (hybrid)
5) Ab7 (Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished)

                                                                                                   69
                           2020 © Jupiter Musical Group LTD. All Rights Reserved
     Basic Harmony: ||                         Bb7             |          %                   |            F7                |           D7               ||   4668




              Option 1: ||                     Bb7             |         Bbm7                 |        Am7                   | G#m7              C#7 ||
                                                                                     Chain of minor 7th chords

     About the Cadence G#m7, C#7 replacing D7:
     Above we have a cadence G#m7, C#7 replacing D7. But in this case we consider it as a simple G#m7 Dorian replacing D7. This chord
     makes part of a chain of consecutive minor 7th chords (Bbm7, Am7, G#m7). We should play hybrid or Dorian ideas over each one of the
     chain of chords. Although we can play G#m7 Dorian ideas over D7, we can also play G#m hybrid ideas over D7 because it will sound
     like a combination between D Altered and D Dominant Diminished Scale. Apart from that, G#m7 lines can give a peculiar flavor to D7
     because the 4th from "G#m7" (C#) is the major 7th of "D".

              Option 4: ||                  Bb7                   |     Ebm7               Ab7          |                Am7                |                  D7               ||
                                                                  Cadence replacing Bb7 (IV)

     About the Cadence Ebm7, Ab7 replacing Bb7:
     Above we have the cadence Ebm7, Ab7 replacing Bb7. However, we should consider it as being a single Ebm7 Dorian or Ebm7 hybrid
     chord. But let's understand step by step where Ebm7 came from. As we know, we can replace a Major Subdominant Region chord (Bb)
     by one of the chords derived from the Minor Subdominant Region (Bbm) in this case we have chosen Gbmaj7 which has the Ebm7 as
     a relative chord.

              Option 5: ||                  Bb7                |           B°                    |    Cm7            F7        |          D7            ||
                                                                                                     Cadence replacing Aø
     About the Cadence Cm7, F7 replacing Aø:
     Above we have the cadence Cm7, F7 replacing Aø. In this case we should consider it as being a single Cm7 Dorian or Cm7 hybrid
     chord. But let's understand step by step where Cm7 came from. First of all we have to remember that Aø is an inversion chord from
     Cm6, which is the same chord as F7(9) chord. Apart from that, Cm7 Dorian contains the same notes as Aø Locrian because both are
     derived from Bb key.

               Major Blues Form

                      PART 3
                           (3rd Story)
                                                   Note:
                                  68


     Notice that in this book we will not focus on the melodic possibilities for the sort turnaround
     cadence in the last two bars of the blues form. Although we have some great ideas of it in some
     examples, we must remember that usually we should breathe in this part in order to give space
                         46




     and separate one story from the other, mainly when we want to anticipate the next chorus.

     However, do not worry about that now, simply analyze and memorize the examples you like the
     most. In the next GB Method books we will have a special chapter focused only on short and
     long turnarounds.

6) Superimposed IIm7/V7/I Cadences over Dominant 7th Chords                                                                                                                4668




Basic Harmony: ||                          Gm7               |             C7                  |        F7                D7       |     Gm7                  C7      ||

         Option 1: ||                     Gm7                |    C#m7              F#7        |        F7                D7       |        Gm7               C7      ||
About the cadence C#m7, F#7 replacing C7:
In this case we have the cadence C#m7, F#7 replacing C7. We can do that because it contains the altered tensions from F7 (#9, b9, #11,
b13). Melodically speaking we can use C#m7 Dorian Scale ideas which will give a different flavor to C7 because of the note "B"(minor
7th from "C#m" and major 7th from "C").

         Option 2: ||                   Gm7                             |    F#m7               B7          |      F7               D7           |        Gm7               C7       ||

About the cadence F#m7, B7 replacing C7:
Above we have a cadence C#m7, F#7 replacing C7 leading to "F" . In this case we should consider this cadence as a single F#m7
Dorian, which can give a special flavour to C7 because of the note "B" (perfect 4th of "F#m7" and major 7th of "C"). As a matter of a
fact, the melodic ideas from F#m7 Dorian or F#m7 hybrid when played over C7, will sound a combination between C7 Dominant
Diminished with C7alt.

                                                                       Cadence replacing C7

About the cadence Abm7, Db7 replacing C7:
Above we have the cadence Abm7,Db7 replacing C7 leading to "F". In this case we should consider this cadence as a single Abm7
Dorian, which can give a special flavor to C7 because of two specific notes: "Cb (B)" and "F" (minor 3rd & major 6th from "Abm7",
and major 7th of & perfect 4th from "C"). Apart from that, Abm7 is part of a minor 7th consecutive "chord chain": Gm7, Abm7, Am7,
which sounds very interesting.
